newsitem.title: UK: Branson glad to be alive after balloon disaster.
newsitem.headline: Branson glad to be alive after balloon disaster.

text.p: British businessman Richard Branson said on Wednesday he was glad to be alive after the balloon in which he was trying to circle the globe began hurtling towards the ground at a dizzying speed of over 40 feet per second.

The night-time plunge -- twice as fast as an express lift -- was only slowed when stand-in co-pilot Alex Ritchie climbed out on to the roof of the capsule and managed to release two ballast tanks to lighten the balloon's load.
Ritchie, wearing a parachute and strapped to the side of the speeding fuselage, carried out his dramatic feat in pitch darkness.
Branson himself also tried to slow the descent by desperately throwing heavy bottles food and fuel out of the fusleage door.
The balloon managed to clear a mountain range and finally landed in the Algerian desert, ending his round-the-world voyage less than 24 hours after it started.

"Alex is the hero of the moment," Branson told his control centre in London. "He saved our lives." Ritchie was a last-minute replacement as co-pilot alongside Per Lindstrand after Rory McCarthy pulled out for health reasons.
Asked if he felt disappointed, Branson said from Algeria: "It's nice to be alive, nice to be sitting here in this incredible desert scenery, and that's really what matters."
The balloon, the Virgin Global Challenger, came down near Bechar, 45 miles (70 km) inside Algeria's border with Morocco and about 400 miles (640 km) from the take-off point in Morocco.
An Algerian military helicopter was quickly on the scene and the British Embassy in Algeria confirmed the three men were safe and well.

The balloon's ascent was driven by helium but the pilots had burners to supplement this lift. At night, helium cools -- causing the balloon to drop -- and officials said the pilots may not have been able to brake the descent with the burners.

"The nature of the problem we are still trying to establish. I honestly can't tell you what it is, except that we know it's a ballast versus helium problem," said project director Mike Kendrick in London.
Branson was in competition with U.S. balloonist Steve Fosset to become the first man to fly round the world in a balloon. Fosset is planning a similar attempt from St. Louis, Missouri.
Virgin officials cast doubt on whether Branson would have enough time to prepare for a second attempt this year. He failed to get off the ground last year because of poor weather.
"I would imagine that we would lose the opportunity to go again in this season, so it will be next year," McCarthy said.

The balloon -- reckoned to be the biggest in the world -- touched ground at 0729 GMT on Wednesday. It had set off under the media spotlight at 1119 GMT on Tuesday from an airfield near the Moroccan city of Marrakesh.

It had headed up into the jetstream that the team had hoped would carry them across North Africa, Saudi Arabia, India, the South China Sea, the Pacific and the United States before landing in Britain after a 24,000-mile (38,600 km) trip expected to take between 14 and 21 days.

Branson, the flamboyant 46-year-old head of the Virgin group of companies, made his name as head of a record retailing and music firm, before developing a successful airline and branching out into products as diverse as condoms and cola.
The tycoon has already crossed the Atlantic and Pacific by balloon.
Branson made a first attempt to enter the record books in 1985, a year after he launched his Virgin Atlantic airline, when he attempted the fastest-ever crossing by boat of the Atlantic.
That time his powerboat capsized 140 miles (220 km) from the British coast and he had to be rescued by helicopter. The next year he achieved his aim with Virgin Atlantic Challenger II.
